title: Gingivitis
blurb: Red, swollen, bleeding gums: what causes gingivitis, how to recognise it, why it is fully reversible and the advice that fixes it.
question: A 24-year-old patient says her gums bleed every time she brushes, so she has started avoiding brushing near them to "let them heal". The dentist notes red, swollen gum margins with plaque along them, and no bone loss. What is the condition, what advice should she get, and can it be fully cured?

teach.body: Gingivitis is inflammation of the gingiva (gums) only. The usual cause is plaque left undisturbed along the gum margin. Its bacteria release toxins, and the body responds by sending extra blood and immune cells to the area. That inflammation makes the gums red, swollen and quick to bleed. Crucially, the deeper supporting tissues, the periodontal ligament and alveolar bone, are not damaged. Remove the plaque and the gums return to full health: gingivitis is completely reversible.

teach.caption: Stippling is the fine 'orange-peel' texture of healthy attached gum. Healthy gums can be naturally pigmented brown in many patients.
The gum is red and swollen, but the bone and periodontal ligament are untouched. Any deepening is a false pocket caused by swelling, not loss of attachment.

teach.h: Gingivitis, and where it can lead
teach.caption: Left: red, swollen gum margins bleeding around the lower incisors, typical of gingivitis. Right: the gum has receded and roots are exposed with dark deposits, changes often seen once disease has progressed to periodontitis.

teach.h: Bleeding is a warning, not a reason to stop
teach.body: Bleeding on brushing is the earliest and most common sign. Many patients then brush less, thinking they're hurting their gums. That makes things worse: more plaque, more inflammation, more bleeding. Advise them to keep brushing gently but thoroughly along the gum line twice a day and to clean between the teeth daily. The bleeding usually settles within a couple of weeks as the gums heal. Bleeding that doesn't settle needs checking by the dentist.

teach.h: Factors that make gums react more
teach.note: These don't cause gingivitis on their own; plaque is still needed. They change how strongly the gums respond to it.

teach.text: Gingivitis has NO loss of attachment and NO bone loss, so it is fully reversible. If a question mentions true pocketing, attachment loss, bone loss or mobility, that is periodontitis, which is not reversible.

items: Gingivitis is inflammation of the gums only, caused by plaque at the gum margin.
Signs: red, swollen, shiny gums that bleed on brushing or probing; usually painless.
No attachment or bone loss: fully reversible with good plaque control.
Advise patients to keep brushing gently; bleeding settles as plaque is controlled.
Management: oral hygiene instruction, scale and polish, review at recall.
Hormones, diabetes, some medicines and smoking modify how the gums react.

summary: You can now explain what causes gingivitis, recognise its signs compared with healthy gums, explain why it is fully reversible, give the right advice to a patient whose gums bleed, list the factors that make gums react more and outline how gingivitis is managed.

A.q: A patient has red, swollen gums that bleed on brushing but don't hurt. The dentist finds plaque at the margins and no bone loss. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A.why: Red, swollen, bleeding but painless gums with plaque and no bone loss are typical of plaque-induced gingivitis.

whyNot.1: Periodontitis involves loss of attachment and bone.
whyNot.2: A periapical abscess comes from a dead pulp and causes pain and swelling at the root tip.
whyNot.3: Necrotising gingivitis is painful, with ulcerated, 'punched-out' papillae.

A.q: Which statement about gingivitis is correct?
options: It involves loss of the alveolar bone
It reverses with good plaque control
A.why: Because no attachment or bone has been lost, the gums return to health once plaque is controlled.

whyNot.0: Not everyone with gingivitis develops periodontitis; it depends on susceptibility and risk factors.
whyNot.1: Bone loss is a feature of periodontitis, not gingivitis.

A.q: A patient says her gums bleed, so she has stopped brushing near them. What is the best advice?
options: Avoid brushing until the bleeding stops
Switch to a hard brush to scrub plaque
Rinse with mouthwash instead of brushing
Keep brushing gently along the gum line
A.why: Bleeding comes from plaque-induced inflammation. Gentle, thorough brushing removes the plaque so the gums can heal.

whyNot.0: Avoiding brushing lets more plaque build up and makes bleeding worse.
whyNot.1: A hard brush and scrubbing can damage the gums.
whyNot.2: Mouthwash can't remove plaque on its own.

B.q: What is the main cause of plaque-induced gingivitis?
options: Brushing too hard with a firm brush
Plaque left at the gum margin
B.why: Bacteria in plaque left along the gum margin trigger the inflammation.

whyNot.0: Hard brushing causes abrasion and recession, not plaque-induced gingivitis.
whyNot.2: Acidic drinks cause erosion of the teeth.

B.q: A pregnant patient notices her gums are bleeding more than usual. What is the best explanation?
options: Pregnancy causes bone loss around the teeth
The baby takes calcium from her teeth
Hormones exaggerate the reaction to plaque
B.why: Pregnancy hormones make the gums react more strongly to plaque, so good plaque control is especially important.

whyNot.0: Pregnancy itself doesn't cause bone loss around the teeth.
whyNot.1: This is a myth: the baby doesn't take calcium from the mother's teeth.

B.q: Which feature would you expect to see in healthy gingiva?
B.why: Healthy gingiva is firm, often stippled, pink (or naturally pigmented), with knife-edge margins.

whyNot.0: Red, rounded margins are signs of inflammation.
whyNot.1: Healthy gums don't bleed on gentle probing.
whyNot.3: Soft, shiny, swollen papillae indicate gingivitis.

C.q: A patient with gingivitis has a probing depth of 4 mm at one site but no bone loss. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Swollen gum creates a false pocket
The junctional epithelium has moved down
C.why: In gingivitis, swelling raises the gum margin, deepening the crevice without any loss of attachment: a false pocket.

whyNot.0: Over-eruption is not a feature of gingivitis.
whyNot.2: Downward movement of the junctional epithelium is attachment loss: a true pocket, seen in periodontitis.

C.q: Which of these is NOT a usual sign of gingivitis?
C.why: Mobility comes from loss of bone and ligament support, which happens in periodontitis, not gingivitis.

whyNot.0: Bleeding on brushing is the classic sign of gingivitis.
whyNot.1: Redness at the margins is a sign of inflammation.
whyNot.3: Swollen papillae are typical of gingivitis.

C.q: What is the most appropriate first management for generalised gingivitis?
options: Oral hygiene advice and a scale
C.why: Gingivitis is caused by plaque, so the answer is better home care plus professional removal of plaque and calculus.

whyNot.1: Antibiotics are not used for plaque-induced gingivitis.
whyNot.2: Surgery isn't needed for a reversible condition.
whyNot.3: Teeth aren't lost in gingivitis; extraction would be wrong.

reteach.title: Like a splinter in your finger
reteach.question: Think about a splinter in your finger. What happens around it, and what happens when you pull it out?

blocks.h: Take out the cause and it heals
blocks.body: Around a splinter the skin goes red, puffy and tender: that's inflammation, your body fighting back. Pull the splinter out and within days the finger heals completely, with no scar. Plaque at the gum margin is the splinter. The red, swollen, bleeding gum is the body fighting it. Remove the plaque every day and the gum heals completely. Leave the 'splinter' in for months or years, though, and damage can spread deeper: that's periodontitis.

blocks.caption: The goal: firm, pink gum hugging the neck of the tooth.

explain.body: Plaque at the gum margin inflames the gingiva. The gums become red, swollen, soft and shiny, and bleed on brushing or probing. It's usually painless, so patients may only notice blood in the sink.

test.q: Which sign of gingivitis is a patient most likely to notice first?
test.why: Bleeding on brushing is the earliest and most common sign, and gingivitis is usually painless.

whyNot.0: Loose teeth come from bone loss in periodontitis.
whyNot.3: New gaps suggest drifting from periodontitis.

explain.body: Only the gum is inflamed. The periodontal ligament and bone are intact and there is no loss of attachment, so removing the plaque lets the tissues return to complete health.

test.q: Why is gingivitis described as reversible?
options: The bacteria die off by themselves
Bone regrows once plaque is removed
No attachment or bone has been lost
It only ever affects young people
test.why: Gingivitis affects only the gum; with no attachment or bone loss, the tissues can fully recover.

whyNot.0: Plaque bacteria keep multiplying unless they are removed.
whyNot.1: No bone has been lost in gingivitis, and lost bone doesn't simply regrow.
whyNot.3: Gingivitis affects people of all ages.

explain.body: Brush twice daily along the gum line with fluoride toothpaste, clean between the teeth every day, and keep going even if the gums bleed at first. The dentist or hygienist removes calculus, and you reinforce the advice at recall.

test.q: Which advice should be reinforced at recall for a patient with gingivitis?
options: Brush twice daily and clean between teeth
Brush once a week with a hard-bristled brush
Stop flossing where the gums bleed
test.why: Twice-daily brushing and daily interdental cleaning remove the plaque that causes gingivitis.

whyNot.1: Weekly brushing is far too little, and hard brushes can damage gums.
whyNot.2: Stopping interdental cleaning leaves plaque between the teeth.
whyNot.3: Mouthwash can't replace mechanical plaque removal.

explain.body: Some factors make the gums react more strongly to the same plaque: pregnancy and puberty hormones, poorly controlled diabetes, smoking (which hides bleeding) and some medicines that cause gum overgrowth.

test.q: Which medicine is associated with gingival overgrowth?
test.why: Phenytoin (an anti-epileptic) is a well-known cause of gingival overgrowth, along with ciclosporin and calcium channel blockers.

whyNot.0: Paracetamol is a painkiller with no effect on gum growth.
whyNot.1: Salbutamol is an asthma reliever inhaler.
whyNot.2: Amoxicillin is an antibiotic and doesn't cause gum overgrowth.
